segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: My name in English is Eddy Bird, E-d-d-y B-i-r-d.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: What is your Cherokee name?

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: Tso-sa-ya is my name.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: Tso-sa-ya.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: My mom got that name from my grandpa. My grandpa, my mom’s dad, his name was Joseph. They called him Tso-sa-ya. That’s where she got it from.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: I’ve heard of my grandpa and my grandma talking about Tso-sa-ya.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: He’s the only one that I didn’t see, but his wife, my mom’s mom, Lin, I’ve seen her.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: Where were you born?

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: Here in Tahlequah, at the old building they called Hastings, by the big school, NSU, that’s where I was born in ’66.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: Where did you grow up?

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: I grew up in Greasy.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: Greasy.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: At first, I remember they called it Zion. I don’t know what they call it in Cherokee. I remember right there, when I was a little boy, there were houses by the school. We were waiting for them to get done building, there in Greasy. When they got done, that’s when we moved to Greasy. That’s where I grew up.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: I think I’ve been around there a few times. My grandma Ke-hi-da used to go see A-ma, and my aunt used to go. We used to go down there, and the old ladies all used to talk Creek.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: They are sisters, and they had brothers, and they were all Creek. Sometimes when I talk Cherokee, I add Creek to it sometimes, and then I got to start back over.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: Sometimes they don’t understand.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: They call that slang, I add that to it.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: You said y’all lived in Zion, and then y’all moved to Greasy.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: I was just six years old when the building at Zion, my mom told me it burnt. For a little while, by Dahlonegah School, when you are coming from that road, when you are coming from the east, there’s a cemetery, and past the bridge, there’s a house on the right in the field. We lived there for a while. She said we moved when they finished the houses.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: Now your work, what do you do? Can you tell us about it?

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: Well, nowadays, some call them 18-wheelers, and some big rigs. That’s what I drive. It’s been many years, let’s see... Really, I’ve been going about 28 years driving them.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: Where? Do you go all over America?

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: I used to, for a long time, but now, where they call towards east, I just go around there. That dog food they call Blue Buffalo dog food, that’s what I take up there, and when I come back, I bring back auto parts. I take it to Tulsa, then I go to Georgia and do the same. I take dog food there. Then I pick stuff up, and I take it close by while I’m finishing up, and then I come back. What I was saying to Jerry, sometimes I come back on Friday nights, but most of the time I come home early Saturday morning when it’s still dark. Then I’m off and leave early Monday.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: You do go all over the place.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: Yeah, I go all over the place.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: Do you leave every week?

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: Yeah, every week. I’ve been to 48 what we call states. But now I go on a dedicated run all the time. I go to two different cities.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: You know what to do and where to go?

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: That, too, and I’ve already thought about where I’m going to stop. I drive all day, and at night I look for a place to park.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: To rest?

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: I rest and sleep, and I start early in the morning.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: So, they know you where you’ve been working so long, and been passing through there? They recognize you when they see you? OK, your family, your brothers, how many are there?

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: Seven of us. Me, I’m the youngest. There would have been eight, but my mom was telling me the first-born got sick when he was just a little boy and died. He would have been three years old. She told me he got sick before he turned three and died. There are four of us boys, and there are two girls.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: I remember them.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: One of them ain’t alive, the one we call Bobby. His name was Ga-li-gi-ni in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: Now, what were your parents’ names?

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: Osi was my dad’s name, and my mom’s was Lizzie. They just called her Lisi.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: You mostly grew up in Greasy?

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: Mostly. On my mom’s side, there was a lot in the family. My mom told me there were two sets of twins born on my mom’s side, and on my dad’s side we counted 12 of them in the family. On my mom’s side, there’s 11. There are a lot living here. Wherever I go, I see my cousin or my second cousin.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: I remember your mom and your dad and K-hi-di.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: How about Mickel, do you ever… And that Eda-Beeb Martha Killer.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: K-hi-di dog.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: Polly’s name was dog.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: I remember them. But it’s been a long time since they passed.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: That one we call Soldier, we call him U-s-ti boy in Cherokee, he’s the only one alive.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: The late Coon.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: The late Coon.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: I remember them. They were funny to listen to when they talked.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: U-s-ti boy is still a joker. He’ll play a prank on you real quick. Sometimes it’s embarrassing, but he don’t mean it that way.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: When they used to throw horseshoes...

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: They still do that where Jody lives.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: We stopped by Jody’s house the other day. He was home.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: They say he’s crippled now.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: Yeah, he told me he had a stroke, when I went and visited him. That book the Cherokees sign, I took it over there. Everybody was there, sitting around. All the family, and the late Johnson was sitting there.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: That’s what I tell my family and my grandkids. Things are different on my dad’s side. Sometimes they don’t include us when they’re doing something, but on my mom’s side, they’re always calling me, or if they’re doing something or gathering or eating, they include us. They are all close. I tell my grandkids that’s how it’s supposed to be. I try to tell them they’re old enough. I take them with me sometimes if they want to go with me. Everywhere we go, I’ll see someone I know. They tell me, “Gaw, Grandpa, you know a lot of people!” When they say, “Who’s that?” I tell them, “They are your cousins.”

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: My family, too, we see a lot of people when we go somewhere. They say they’re our cousins, but I don’t know if they can all be admitted.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: That’s true, some of them don’t know, do they?

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: No, and some of them deny that they’re your cousins. That’s not good.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: When they owe you, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: When they don’t pay.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: The ones that don’t pay, they will go around facing the other way.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: That’s what I tell them. I say, “If you don’t want to see anyone, give them $10, and you won’t ever see them again.”

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: That’s true.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: They’ll disappear forever.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: And if you want to see someone you haven’t seen in a long time, go to Wal-Mart. You’ll see them there.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: That’s true. How about now? Can you tell me if you remember your grandma and grandpa?

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: Just a little.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: Just a little?

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: My grandma and my grandpa, my dad’s parents, I remember them just a little bit. U-ni-wi was my dad’s dad, and my grandma’s name was Que-di. Betty and John were their names. I remember my grandma. We used to go eat there all the time at my grandma’s house or my aunt’s house. But most of the time we’d go to my grandma’s…’cause when we were little, we went to school. When we got out of school, when we were hungry, we were told to go there, to my grandma’s. I remember U-ni-wi just a little bit. Where they call Lees Creek towards Rock Fence Church, about three miles from the big road going up the hill, they owned that. He used to grow…we used to like what they call popcorn. We would pop them, I remember that. I was seven, no six years old when my grandpa passed away.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: I don’t remember him. I’ve never heard of him before.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: He was tall.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: Was he tall?

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: How about Wesley? We called him Sonny, the crippled one. Did you know him?

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: You never saw him? They say they looked alike.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: Really? The other ones you’re saying, like Lin and Tso-sa, I don’t remember them, but my grandpa would mention them sometimes when they were living. But my grandma knew all of them. Sometimes they would remember people.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: My grandma Lin, that you’re saying Lin, she was a twin, that I remember. Her sister’s name was Jokie. Her English name was Jenny.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: What you’re saying, Jokie, that’s a Creek word for ‘little girl.’ Yeah, that’s what they used to call this girl in Marble City. They call her Jokie, I remember that. For one thing, they don’t allow to talk about something that I was telling you about. What about your name that is wrote down? You told me it was Bird while ago. You wouldn’t know where they got that?

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: My mom told me that a long time ago, Stanley Shall’s wife Nadine, she was my dad’s cousin. Their name was Longbird a long time ago. I don’t know why they changed it. The ones from Muskogee and like Joe Byrd, my mom used to say they were my cousins, too, but I really don’t know. My mom used to tell me everything, and I forgot it all.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: I think I’ve heard about it. My grandma used to say she called him Ned, I think. Ned Longbird or Bill Longbird. She said they used to live there a long time ago. They might have been your cousins, too.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: They probably were.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: My grandma’s name was Bird, too.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: I think that’s what they used to say and then...

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: We might be related, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: We might be.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: Don’t be borrowing money.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: Better be paying back if I loan you money.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: I’ll come back Friday.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: And another thing, my grandma’s grandpa’s name was Baby Bird. I think that’s where that comes from. How about a nickname, do they call you by anything?

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: In English?

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: Either way. Cherokee.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: They just call me Birdman.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: Oh, Birdman.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: It started when I was little. My family, they call me Ed.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: Oh, Ed. Where did you get that they call you Ed?

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: They just made Eddy short. Most of them just say, “Hey.” My name is Hey. Sometimes, when they say, “Hey,” I turn around.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: How about, do you know anything you would like to say about your family? Something funny, or you might remember anything that’s important to you that you like to talk about all the time?

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: I’ll tell y’all one. When I was little, my mom told me I didn’t know I was saying that... It’s funny - them houses that are next to us, well, there are six houses real close, and when we was little kids, we used to play at all of them. At one house, there used to be a lot of room on the front porch. We used to play right there. One time, there was a scorpion. My mom said, “Have y’all seen it?” to that Kenny Vann, Johnson Vann’s son. Kenny told me to watch out. She said he said, “Look out, Eddy, there’s a scorpion right there.” I told him, “Huh-uh, Daddy said that was almost a crawdad.” She said, “You really meant it, too. You were arguing with Kenny about what it was called but it was a stinger,” she said. I was telling them my dad said it was almost a crawdad.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: Scorpion.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: Scorpion. That’s how I grew up with the name Scorpion. “Huh-uh, Daddy said that was almost a crawdad.” That’s what I told them, and they laughed.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: That’s good. How about that - do you remember, you’ve heard it everywhere, you might know something about the Cherokee Trail of Tears from the east. You might know something your parents told you, or your grandma. You might know something, or someone said something. You might know something about how the Cherokees got sent off?

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: My mom never told me anything like that, but my sisters got married and these Black people were involved. When they left, as they were going, the ones we call Freeman, there’s a few of them in there that are close relatives to a few of my family. Their dads were members of them, I was told. The late Ice and the late Bill and Johnson and their sister, their family. The oldest, I forget his name.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: Backing up.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: Yeah, that, too. Just how they look they looked like them, but their skin wasn’t that dark. That’s all I know, but my mom tells it how she heard. She says they came poor. She used to say to me, “A lot of them got sick.” That’s all I know.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: How about you might know something, or heard something about the North and South fighting a long time ago. Maybe someone in your family was in it?

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: Not really, just that one my mom told me about. My mom was the only one who told me about stuff like that. “Your cousins joined the Army and before they went to war,” my mom told me, “they would use medicine on themselves.” I guess they would blow medicine on themselves so the bullets would miss them while they were flying around. My mom said that’s what kind of medicine they put on themselves.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: I’ve heard my grandpa talking about that sometime ago. The late U-ni-s was in the war. He said, “I guess they knew something. They put medicine on themselves and as the bullets were flying they were melting.”

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: That’s it, yeah.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: The bullets were melting before they reached them, he was saying. There were melted bullets everywhere. He was saying that they stole horses while the enemy was sleeping. They would go there and take all their horses, and when they got up, they didn’t have any horses.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: They didn’t know what to do.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: He said they didn’t know what to do. Then he said that there was one who was a real wise man. He was saying the North was on that side and the South on this side. And he said he was running around in the middle. He would turn around and come back and run around doing his arms like this [gesture]. He said they couldn’t never do anything to him ’cause he was such a wise man. I forget his name. My grandpa used to say it. He said they would hire him to go run and check out where they was fighting, then they would go there.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: They had him as the reporter.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: His elderly grandpa said that. That’s what I knew. I figured you would know something.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: I’ve never heard anything like that before.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: How about when the Cherokees were given the restricted land a long time ago? Do you know anything?

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: No, I don’t know nothing about that. There’s a lot, like I was saying a while ago, my mom probably told me about it. We would sit on the porch by ourselves, that’s what I remember. I was always getting chased off ’cause I was always listening to them talking. They would tell me, “Go play or go outside where the kids are.” That’s how I think I learned how to talk Cherokee good. But about that, she probably told me. She knew a lot, and we were saying, E-di-bid, he told me a lot, but I forgot.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: Can you tell or picture it how it was where you grew up, at like that school at Greasy? Can you tell how things are, like the valleys or the roads?

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: I remember they were dirt, and the roads weren’t that wide. When we got there back then, all of us kids used to ride bicycles on the roads. We used to go all the way up where they call Beaver Gap, and we had trails in the woods, too. Where the Greasy School Building is, just below it, we had a place to swim, and then I think Lees Creek... no, it’s Sallisaw Creek, that’s where it went to, Sallisaw. We made a little trail so when we wanted to go swimming, we would go that way. And like what I’m saying, over there by the school below it, that’s where we’d go fishing.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: That’s close to the dam.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: We went swimming towards the dam. There were a lot of big rocks - big. That’s where our own locker rooms were. That’s where we put our shorts, and when we got there, we put them on, changed our clothes. It was there when we were walking one time... I don’t know the name of it in Cherokee, but it was a snake. We thought we had seen a cobra, but it was just that Spread Nanner A.K.A. Hognose Snake or what are they called? We saw that man, and we took off running. We didn’t stop till we got home. We were saying ‘man’ but we saw a cobra. We were on the trail, and it crossed. It stood up to its neck when we got close, and it screamed and made a sound. Boy, we thought we seen a cobra.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: That’s what happened to me, too. One time, I was just a little boy then. My grandma asked me to go get something. She said, “Go to your aunt’s and get it.” I was walking when I saw it. It was laying there in my path. I was watching and I was thinking, “What am I going to do?” I was thinking, “Boy, it looks scary.” I was scared, so I turned back around. I told my grandma, “I met that kind of snake.” She started laughing. She told me, “There ain’t snakes like that around here.” She told me, “You saw that qua-hna-da-yo/Spread Nanner.” She told me, “That kind will spit on you.” It looked like it was dangerous, and I was scared.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: Where are you saying? We’ve been everywhere down in the...

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: Valley.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: Valley, yeah, and just climbing on the mountain. We were always doing something, and we would climb trees when we were little. Two or three of us would climb to the very top, and we would bend it, and someone standing on the ground would grab it, and we’d ride it like a horse, bouncing it and pretending it was a horse. We would hold it, and we would be hollering, “Yeee-haaaww!” That was fun, and nowadays, the kids don’t know nothing about that.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: No, they don’t. They don’t know nothing. That’s what we used to do, too. One time we would say, “Pick a tree to climb.” I picked one that big [gesture]. I went to the top and it was just going like this [gesture]. When I got halfway up there, it broke.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: There where you’re saying, when it snowed, we played on the hills, too. We were always looking for something to do when we were little. When we didn’t have anything to do, if we found some tires somewhere, we would roll those around everywhere, and we’d put dust in them. One time, I found some hubcaps. I put them on both sides, and I was walking around with a grin. Our hands would turn black when we rolled them tires around all day long.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: Kids won’t do that now.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: They wouldn’t know. They’ll just say, “Eeewww!”

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: I tell them at work, I’ve been to the woods, deep in the valleys and mountains. My kids, as they were growing up, they didn’t know nothing about that. When I was this tall [gesture], I was already in the woods. About your neighbors, can you tell me who they were?

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: What I was telling you a while ago, Johnson Vann and Mary Vann lived on the first turnoff. There were three houses on the left, and on the right there were three houses. Johnson and Mary Vann lived in the first house there, and my mom and dad lived in the second house. And then at the end of the road, Nadine and Stanley lived there. Across from Stanley, his dad Charlie lived there. I forget his name in Cherokee, he lived there. And coming back, Steeler Shell lived there. Steeler was a cop a long time ago. He had green eyes and he was tall. His skin was kind of dark, too. He was tall.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: They say he lives towards Jay.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: Steeler Shell?

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: He’s passed away long time ago.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: I guess I’m thinking about somebody else.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: And right beside them, K-he-di and Will lived there where Jody lived.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: OK. You done told me how everything was there?

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: And you told me how this was, too, already.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: I really liked it when as soon as we got out of school in the evening, after I got through eating, they gave me a bicycle one time. And that all the time…I had roads everywhere by myself. I liked playing by myself. I had roads everywhere and I had those, they call them ramps, everywhere. I was acting like the BMX Bandit. I was doing it like this [gesture] when I went up, till I ran into a tree. For real, I’m not lying, the handlebar broke. I felt heavy. My mom asked, “What happened?” I started crying. All of my family, well, all of my cousins were living there. Then, going down the hill, George Bunch and my aunt they called Sa-la-di built a house.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: OK. What is your favorite thing to eat like food? What do you think is the best thing you like?

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: Well, I still like beans and boiled potatoes and fried bread. That’s what I like best. My wife learned how to make that stuff. That’s why I told her, “I think I’ll keep you.” I told her, “I guess we’ll live together.” That’s what I still like the most. I like it better when they cook breakfast anytime, even in the evening. That’s what she makes for me, that is what I like the best - eggs and bacon. That’s what I like the best.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: About that, a long time ago, what the old people ate, nowadays, we don’t eat that, or a lot of them don’t eat that anymore. Can you tell me what you like to eat that grew in the woods?

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: Nowadays, I don’t eat that, but when I was growing up, my mom used to like to fix that watercress and poke salad, and the thing she liked to eat the most was lettuce. She loved to make that. Every time I got back home she would have that on the table. Well, she would have it put up, but when I got there, she would heat it up, and we would eat that. The thing she liked most and I still want to eat, that is that wild onion. When my mom was alive, and when she passed away, that’s the last time I ate some. I really want to eat some of that. And I remember that commodity that’s what kept us alive all the time growing up. When you think about it, everything they made was put together, and it was good. But everything my mom made to eat, she made it without gravy all the time. I learned that. At first I didn’t like it what they call mustard, what the Creeks eat, my mom would put grease in it and eat it. And she would make gravy out of coffee – red-eye gravy. That’s the kind of stuff I remember, and she would have biscuits put up, and whatever we didn’t eat up, she covered up with a sheet, and it would be sitting there. And sometimes, even though Mom and Dad were working, neighbors, the late K-hi-di and Wi-I-la, used to have chickens, and sometimes we would eat eggs all the time. That’s where I learned how to make fried eggs.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: Your mom did most of the cooking? OK, you talked about the food that lives in the woods and it comes out in the spring.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: Spring, the rest of it came out in the spring. And I remember that my mom and them would be joking around with each other. When it was just this tall [gesture], they would still be looking for it, picking it. And when they came back, they told how it was outside: “It’s still getting cold, it’s going to snow.” They would tell each other, “It’s ’cause y’all are looking for that onion.”

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: That’s what they were saying the other day. I was talking to my mom. I said, “They’re saying it’s going to snow,” and she said, “I know. They are already looking for onion down the valley.” They’re going down there, I’m watching them go down there, and she said, “It’s really going to snow.” Boy, it wasn’t very long - the next morning, it was already white. It was sleeting bad and raining. She said, “That’s who’s making it cold.”

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: That one we call E-di-bid, she likes walnut. She used to make kanuchi real good, that one. Man, it was really good. I don’t know when I drunk that last. I miss that.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: Me, too. Here recently, when they built this and they had a big opening, a lot of the Cherokee speakers came and had a meeting, and they had kanuchi. Me and my mom drank some.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: And you didn’t tell me?

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: I thought I told you. OK, we already know about what they cooked and what they put in, like eggs and onion. We know what you said about the coffee gravy. OK, about this is how it’s written. When you speak Cherokee, who do they say you sound like when they listen to you talk?

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: Gah-lee, I don’t want to tell about that. Nobody has really said anything like that. I’ve never heard it before, but wherever I go, wherever I get to, they know I’m Cherokee, even if they are White people, ’cause I speak Cherokee. Then they would say, “I wish I could talk Cherokee.” They think about U-s-ti. Boy, they told me about his laughs, and that he was a prankster wherever he went.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: Does your family have anything y’all say? Or y’all might do something to recognize? Maybe your family has something to say to each other?

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: Haw… We just joke around when we get together. We talk about when we was little. We don’t really have anything to say to ourselves. How about when you done this, how about when you was little and done this, that’s what we talk about. We have fun when we all get together. It’s joyful that we still love one another.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: That’s true. Now in the future, we might talk about something. Nowadays, that me and you are talking Cherokee. In about 20 years in the future, I don’t know how it’s going to be like then. I don’t know if I’m even going to be alive.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: I don’t know either. It would be good.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: It would be good, that’s what I say, too. We don’t know about tomorrow, but do you ever think about how it’s going to be, to talk then? When you think about it, do you ever think about it? Can you tell us about it?

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: That’s true, I think about it all the time. I’m not lying, I’m thinking about it. When I’m home by myself, I try to teach my family and my wife. I was telling the teachers a while ago, “I’ve never thought about it when I was little, and when I became an adult, I never believed or didn’t think that Cherokee language would run out.” Now I laugh when I talk Cherokee. When I talk to my wife or when she says something, we just laugh. She would be teasing me, saying, “You act like you’re the last Cherokee.” She would say, “You’re not the only Cherokee around, there’s a lot of Cherokee speakers,” and then we would talk about that. But really, my heart feels heavy. I think, “I hope it don’t run out.” I think, “Who am I going to see that speaks Cherokee when I get older?” And when I look at the newspaper, a long time ago, about five years ago, when I used to teach the kids, and when they finished, I think I would like to see them somewhere. I wonder, “Do they still speak Cherokee?” Some of them became really good speakers. This is what I was saying to them, “I would like to see you sometimes or meet you somewhere.” Or I might meet someone somewhere. I want it to be like that. I would like to hear them talk Cherokee.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: I’ve thought the same thing. When we first started working here, there wasn’t that much to think about what we’re talking about here. I think the same thing you’re thinking. I used to think all the Cherokee speakers were going to live peacefully. Then when we started working here - we wanted to start working here, and when it opened up, we got hired here. We were coming in the morning, and saying, “In about 50 or 40 years, I wonder how it’s going to be to talk Cherokee.” My aunt, she got quiet and thought about it for a long time. And then she said, “I will be over 100 years old,” she said, “Your mom is going to be really old, and you will be 90 almost to a 100 years old.” She just got quiet right there and then. We said, “We’re not going to be alive.” She gave me something to think about.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: For real.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: I thought, “I wonder how it’s going to be in the future.” We almost cried.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: That’s true, it’ll make you cry. I told them I’m glad I grew up speaking Cherokee.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: Me too.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: Wherever I go, they know. Whoever it is, they know me, that I’m Cherokee, and what we’re talking about I’ve never thought about it, but now I think about it, it’s coming to me. These that are going to school and this building, when I was telling them, I said, “Don’t ever quit learning, every day, all day, when you’re alive.” I told them, “When you think about it, tell yourself or think, ‘I’m Cherokee, I am Cherokee, I speak Cherokee’.” Wherever you go, even if it’s the first person you see, ’cause that’s how I am. I don’t know if that’s good, but I don’t care. “I’m Cherokee,” I’ll say, “O-si-yo.” That’s what I told them. “You’re going to know when you meet someone who is a speaker. How they speak and how they talk - that’s when you’re going to use Cherokee.” Really, these buildings someone how y’all are doing this somebody else like one of these students, it would be good if they picked it up and thought, “I would like to do the same thing.” That’s the only way it’s going to keep going. And as they are learning, if they really mean it, it will happen. I think about it all the time. When I used to teach the little kids, I think it would have been good if I kept doing it. I’m getting old, and I think about it. I don’t want the Cherokee language to run out. I think it would be good if somebody picked it up so they can teach it. What I was telling them, when they get out of school here, the learners would learn a lot more in everything they read in Cherokee. That’s the only way they are going to learn more. And in everything you learn, it will be joyful. “This is what I learned, gaw, I’m going to tell the teacher when I see him/her.” You will feel happy that way. Like I was telling the other teacher. Really, when it comes from the person’s heart, whatever they are thinking, that’s what’s going to happen. And passing by on these roads, looking this way, it looks pretty. I think, “Man, the Cherokees come from a long way. And now they got their own school.” To me, my heart feels at ease that I’m Cherokee. That’s why I wanted to look at it and look around. God made it good for me to come here today.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: OK, can you tell me what you think about it? Sometimes I think the same way. In the future, in about 20 years, how do you think it’s going to be then when our grandkids - your grandkids and my grandkids - how are they going to be? What are they going to be doing? Have you ever thought about that?

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: It’s scary when you think about it. It gets scary, it scares me. The reason why I think about that stuff is there’s a lot of stuff that ain’t supposed to happen, but is happening nowadays. There’s a lot of mean and angry people from far off who are coming to America. Wherever I go, there’s a lot more people from far away. Just the other day, I was telling them, “When my grandkids lived with me, I talked to them all the time, or when they ask something, I instruct them.” It would be nice if somebody good... if these girls could find a nice man, and it better be a man, too. I don’t know if that’s good. Someone that thinks right, ’cause there’s still some around ’cause there’s a lot happening and it’s changing. We see it all the time. This what we call social media world, that’s what the kids are watching more these days. What they see, they are trying to do. That’s why, myself and my cousins, I tell them it’s none of my business what y’all do, but I tell y’all this ’cause I love y’all. I just hope things are good where they can understand the good and the bad.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: Where they can work good.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: Yeah, where they can work. They tell me, “This is what I want to work, or this is what I want to be,” and then I tell them again, “As long as I don’t know what you’re going to be. But if you work and if you’re getting a check, that’s what’s important. If you don’t have any money, you can’t buy anything that you want.” When I think about children, me and my wife talk about it all the time, it would be nice if they find someone or friends or find a good job, as long as… My late father, he would tell me, “Don’t worry about it if you’re having a hard time money-wise, as long as you’re working somewhere, you’re going to be getting paid.” And he would tell me, “Nobody is going to give you anything.” That’s what I see nowadays.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: Same with me. I have a lot of grandkids, and that’s what I tell them. “Y’all learn real good and go to school, and when you’re working, don’t owe anywhere.” I tell them it’s the way it’s supposed to be. That’s what I tell them - the only place I owe is IRS.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: My mom used to say that to me too. Don’t just be buying anything. Something you really need if you can, if you’re able to do it for them or do it for others.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: About that, all that’s written. I wonder how it’s going to be like in the future for themselves. We’ve talked about how it is on the outside, how it is to look around. What are they looking for? OK, this is the last one. It got a little different for me. Where it’s a wooded area, in about 25 years, how do you think the world is going to be then?

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: It would be nice if we could still see the woods. They are building houses everywhere now and when they cut the trees down, they are not planting another one. Like you mention, wherever I go, I look around and I see there’s a lot more houses. They’re building more nowadays. Back when we were growing up, what we call country roads, there’s not that many of them anymore. When it gets to that time, these gas powered vehicles, I don’t know if there will be some around, or maybe it will be just the ones you plug in. The reason why it’s the climate control. There’s a lot of that stuff going on. Some of them don’t believe that those smokehouses and the factories where the smoke goes up, that really is messing up our breathing. When it comes that time, it would be nice if I’m still alive. If I can understand my mind, I don’t know what I will be thinking about. I don’t know how I will be living then. It would be nice if I could still live. As the years go by, a lot changes. Like what I’m saying, everywhere I go I see it: the stuff we bought a long time ago, a shirt or a part to fix a car, we went to the store and bought it, ain’t it? And now, you can order it sitting at your house. That’s what’s going on more, now. They’re building them everywhere, these what we call Amazon. I see storages everywhere. Maybe there’s not a lot of wooded areas now. There’s mostly houses, that’s what I see.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: One time, me and my mom were sitting at home. Squirrels were running around everywhere. I told her, “Gaw, a long time ago, we were hunting them everywhere.” She said, “Yeah, that’s true, and now, they’re climbing around everywhere right there.” I asked her, “How come?” And this is what she said: “This used to be all woods right here. I lived in town, Tahlequah. It used to be all woods here. We are the ones that came where the squirrels live.”

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: That’s true.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: Nowadays, them big cities, they’re getting bigger. Then they say the animals that live in the woods come around. My mom said, “Huh-uh, we’re the ones going to the woods,” when me and my mom were talking.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: She was telling the truth, ain’t it? When we’re watching TV, sometimes they’ll show that they see a bear by the houses, or deer walking around in town. We’re the ones that messed it up. Man is messing up the world and the woods, without caring about it. It’s the money they are chasing the most.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: Where I live, over there by the big school, whenever I leave in the morning, it’s still dark, and a deer is always crossing. I think that’s how much the town multiplied - where the deer used to go when it was all woods.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: You said it right. Me too, behind…right by the road 51 highway, I think it’s called Roberts. I live across from there, and behind there they’re always there. And them big cats, big bobcats and fox, we see a lot of them behind there, and deer, and there’s a lot of skunks. That’s what I see. When it comes to that time, if we’re still alive, I believe we’re all going to see that.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: At my house where I live, there are some skunks there, too. They go under the house. That one time in Marble - I’m going to tell something funny. My boy, he was this tall [gesture]. He went out and I guess there was a skunk around somewhere. He came in and said, “Dad, there’s a skunk around somewhere, ’cause I smell it farting.” OK, Eddy, we’re finishing up talking. I have to go over there real fast when we’re done, but you might tell these sitting here something. I finished everything. We looked at what we was supposed to look at and talk about. Somebody is waiting for me, but when you get done, go around right there [gesture]. You know where my room is? I’ll be in there. I have to go there real fast. Some woman who speaks Cherokee has come here and wants to sign. Have you done that?

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: I already signed it.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: Oh, OK.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: I appreciate you.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: OK.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: Let’s talk again. When I get done here, I’m going to go visit Phillis.

segments.speaker: david-crawler
segments.translation: OK, Eddy, I’m glad we talked.

segments.speaker: eddie-bird
segments.translation: [gesture].
